subtopics.name: Income Statement & Statement of Financial Position

parts.problem_md:
A manufacturer calculated the cost of production for the year at \$54 500.

It was found that insurance and rates, \$3 400, had been omitted from the financial statements.

Insurance and rates is allocated 80% to the factory and 20% to the offices.

What was the correct cost of production?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The cost of production includes direct costs and indirect costs (factory overheads)

  - costs relating to the offices are not included in the cost of production
  - they will be included as expenses in the income statement
- Calculate the amount of insurance and rates that is allocated to the factory

  - 80% × \$3 400 = \$2 720
- Add this cost to the current cost of production

  - \$54 500 + \$2 720 = \$57 220

**A** is incorrect; the insurance and rates allocated to the factory have been incorrectly subtracted from the current cost of production

**B** is incorrect; the insurance and rates allocated to the offices (instead of those allocated to the factory) have been incorrectly added to the current cost of production

**D** is incorrect; the full amount for insurance and rates has been added to the current cost of production, even though office expenses should not included be in the cost of production

parts.problem_md:
A manufacturer’s inventory of raw materials at the start of the year was valued at \$1 500. At the end of the year, it was valued at \$1 250.

What was the effect of this decrease on the cost of production and the cost of sales?

|   | cost of production | cost of sales |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | decrease | decrease |
| **B** | increase | increase |
| **C** | increase | no change |
| **D** | no change | increase |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The cost of raw materials consumed

  - = opening inventory of raw materials
  - + purchases of raw materials
  - - closing inventory of raw materials
- As the opening inventory is bigger than the closing inventory the overall effect is an increase in the cost of raw materials
- Cost of production

  - = prime cost
  
    - this includes the cost of raw materials consumed
  - + factory overheads
  - + work in progress at the start of the year
  - - work in progress at the end of the year
- An increase in the cost of raw materials consumed causes an increase in the cost of production
- Cost of sales

  - = opening inventory of finished goods
  - + cost of production
  - - closing inventory of finished goods
- An increase in the cost of production causes an increase in the cost of sales
- Therefore both the cost of production and the cost of sales increase

**A** is incorrect; this would have been the answer if the closing inventory was greater than the opening inventory

**C** is incorrect; if the cost of production increases then the cost of sales increases

**D** is incorrect; this would have been the answer if the inventories were referring to finished goods rather than raw materials

parts.problem_md: Which calculation gives the cost of the raw materials consumed?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- To calculate the cost of raw materials consumed:

  - start with the opening inventory of raw materials
  
    - these were used during the current year
  - add the purchases of raw materials
  
    - these are additional raw materials purchased throughout the year
  - add the carriage inwards
  
    - this is the delivery cost of the raw materials
  - subtract the closing inventory of raw materials
  
    - these have not yet been used and therefore should be subtracted from this year's cost
- opening inventory of raw materials + purchases of raw materials + carriage inwards - closing inventory of raw materials

**A** is incorrect; the opening and closing inventories of raw materials are the wrong way around

**B** is incorrect; the opening and closing inventories of raw materials are the wrong way around and the carriage inwards has been incorrectly subtracted

**D** is incorrect; the carriage inwards has been incorrectly subtracted

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: closing inventory of raw materials + purchases of raw materials + carriage inwards - opening inventory of raw materials

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: closing inventory of raw materials + purchases of raw materials - carriage inwards - opening inventory of raw materials

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: opening inventory of raw materials + purchases of raw materials + carriage inwards - closing inventory of raw materials

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: opening inventory of raw materials + purchases of raw materials - carriage inwards - closing inventory of raw materials

parts.problem_md:
A manufacturing company provided the following information.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| cost of raw materials | 162 000 |
| factory rent | 31 000 |
| direct wages | 83 000 |
| factory supervisor's salary | 28 000 |
| depreciation of machinery | 35 000 |
| machinery repairs | 10 000 |

What was the prime cost of manufacturing?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The prime cost is the total of the direct costs

  - direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses
- Determine whether each cost is direct or indirect

  - raw materials is a direct cost
  - factory rent is an indirect cost
  - direct wages are a direct cost
  - factory supervisor's salary is an indirect cost
  - depreciation of machinery is an indirect cost
  - machinery repairs are an indirect cost
- Add together the direct costs

  - \$162 000 + \$83 000 = \$245 000

**A** is incorrect; it is missing the direct wages

**C** is incorrect; this has incorrectly included the factory supervisor's salary (the factory supervisor is not directly linked to the production of the goods)

**D** is incorrect; this is the total of all the direct and indirect costs

parts.problem_md: Which calculation is used by a manufacturer to find the cost of production?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The cost of production is the total cost to produce the goods

  - start with the prime cost
  
    - this is the total of the direct costs
  - add the factory overheads
  
    - these are the indirect costs
  - add the opening work in progress
  
    - this is the work that was not completed at the start of the year
  - subtract the closing work in progress
  
    - this is the work that has not been completed during the year so subtract it as it will be completed in the following year
- prime cost + factory overheads + opening work in progress - closing work in progress

**B** is incorrect; factory overheads increase the cost of production so should be added

**C** is incorrect; the opening and closing works in progress are the wrong way around

**D** is incorrect; the opening and closing works in progress are the wrong way around and the factory overheads should be added

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: prime cost + factory overheads + opening work in progress - closing work in progress

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: prime cost - factory overheads + opening work in progress - closing work in progress

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: prime cost + factory overheads - opening work in progress + closing work in progress

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: prime cost - factory overheads - opening work in progress + closing work in progress

parts.problem_md: Which calculation gives the prime cost for a manufacturing business?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The prime cost is the total of the direct costs

  - Direct costs are made up of materials, labour and expenses

**A** is incorrect; it is missing direct expenses

**C** is incorrect;  factory overheads are indirect costs and therefore do not contribute to the prime cost

**D** is incorrect; it is missing direct expenses and it incorrectly includes factory overheads

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: direct material + direct labour + direct expenses

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: direct material + direct labour + direct expenses + factory overheads

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: direct material + direct labour + factory overheads

parts.problem_md: What would be included in the statement of financial position of a manufacturing business but not a wholesale business?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Work in progress only applies to manufacturing businesses

  - This is the work that has been started to create goods but that is not yet complete

**A **is incorrect; machinery could be owned by any type of business

**B** is incorrect;  office equipment can be owned by any type of business

**C** is incorrect; any type of business can have trade payables

parts.problem_md:
A manufacturing business started on 1 May 2023.  The owner provided the following information about the first year in business.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| prime cost | 65 420 |
| factory overheads | 17 270 |
| work in progress at the end of the year | 2 050 |
| closing inventory of finished goods | 2 870 |

What was the cost of production?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Cost of production

  - = prime cost
  - + factory overheads
  - + work in progress at the start of the year
  - - work in progress at the end of the year
- This is the first year of business so there is no work in progress at the start of the year
- Note that the closing inventory of finished goods does not affect the cost of production
- \$65 420 + \$17 270 + \$0 - \$2 050 = \$80 640

**A** is incorrect; the closing inventory of finished goods has also been subtracted

**B** is incorrect;  the closing inventory of finished goods has been subtracted instead of the work in progress at the end of the year

**D** is incorrect; the work in progress at the end of the year has been added not subtracted

parts.problem_md:
A manufacturing business provided the following information for a financial year.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| purchases of raw material | 95 000 |
| carriage inwards on raw material | 3 000 |
| opening inventory of raw material | 36 000 |
| closing inventory of raw material | 28 000 |

What was the cost of raw materials consumed?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Cost of raw materials consumed

  - = opening inventory of raw material
  - + purchases of raw material
  - + carriage inwards on raw materials
  - - closing inventory of raw material
- \$36 000 + \$95 000 + \$3 000 - \$28 000 = \$106 000

**A** is incorrect; the carriage inwards has not been included and the inventory values are the wrong way around

**B** is incorrect;  the inventory values are the wrong way around (the opening has been subtracted and the closing has been added)

**C** is incorrect; the carriage inwards has not been included

parts.problem_md:
A manufacturer provided the following information at the end of his financial year.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| work in progress at the start of the year | 5 400 |
| work in progress at the end of the year | 4 600 |
| prime cost | 87 200 |
| factory overheads | 19 500 |

What was the cost of production for the year?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The prime cost is the total of the direct costs
- Factory overheads are the indirect costs
- Cost of production

  - = prime cost
  - + factory overheads
  - + work in progress at the start of the year
  - - work in progress at the end of the year
- \$87 200 + \$19 500 + \$5 400 - \$4 600 = \$107 500

**A** is incorrect; the factory overheads have been subtracted instead of added and the work in progress values are the wrong way around

**B** is incorrect; the factory overheads have been subtracted instead of added

**C** is incorrect; the work in progress values are the wrong way around (the start has been subtracted and the end has been added)

parts.problem_md:
A manufacturing business provided the following information for the year ended 31 May 2024.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| depreciation of machinery | 13 000 |
| raw materials consumed | 62 000 |
| wages of machine operators | 31 000 |
| salaries of factory supervisors | 28 000 |
| rent of factory | 12 000 |

What was the total of the direct costs?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Direct costs are directly linked to the production of the goods

  - wages of machine operators and raw materials consumed are direct costs
  - depreciation, rent and salaries of factory supervisors are indirect costs
- Total = \$62 000 + \$31 000 = \$93 000

**B** is incorrect; this includes rent

**C **is incorrect; this includes rent and depreciation

**D** is incorrect; this is the total of all the costs

parts.problem_md:
Which costs of a manufacturing business are indirect costs?

1. rent of the factory
2. wages of employees who make the goods
3. wages of the factory supervisors
4. raw materials used in production
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Indirect costs are not directly linked to the production of the goods

  - rent of the factory is an indirect cost
  - wages of employees who make the goods is a direct cost
  - wages of the factory supervisors is an indirect cost
  - raw materials used in production is a direct cost

**B** is incorrect; these are the direct costs

**C** is incorrect; the wages of employees who make the goods is a direct cost

**D** is incorrect; the wages of the factory supervisors is also an indirect cost because the supervisors are not directly linked to the production of the goods

parts.problem_md: Where is work-in-progress shown in the statement of financial position of a manufacturing business?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- All stages of goods are included in the current assets section

  - raw materials
  - work in progress
  - finished goods

**A**, **C** and **D** are incorrect

parts.problem_md:
Sara owns a clothing factory. She sells the clothing to a small number of local shops. She allows 30 days credit.

At 30 September 2023, Sara’s ledger account balances included the following.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| Inventory at 1 October 2022 |   |
| Raw materials | 4 875 |
| Work in progress | 8 125 |
| Finished goods | 12 890 |
| Purchases of raw materials | 56 400 |
| Wages |   |
| Machine operators | 43 300 |
| Factory supervisor | 25 000 |
| Delivery vehicle driver | 14 250 |
| Rates and insurance | 29 600 |
| General factory expenses | 9 650 |
| Factory machinery – at cost | 80 000 |
| Factory machinery – provision for depreciation | 35 000 |
| Trade receivables | 27 000 |
| Cash at bank | 1 050 |

Additional information

1. Inventory at 30 September 2023

| Raw material | 5 110 |
|---|---|
| Work in progress | 7 365 |
| Finished goods | 13 725 |

2. At 30 September 2023 general factory expenses of \$335 were unpaid.
3. Insurance of \$8 000 had been paid for the year July 2023 to June 2024.
4. Rates and insurance are to be apportioned equally 
between the factory and the office.
5. Factory machinery is depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method

**REQUIRED**

Prepare Sara’s manufacturing account for the year ended 30 September 2023

Sara 
Manufacturing Account for the year ended 30 September 2023

|---|---|---|

|   |   |   |

|   |   |   |
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   |
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the adjusted figure for general factory expenses

- Add on the accrued expense

$9650+335=9985$

Calculate the adjusted figure for rates and insurance

- Calculate the amount paid in advance Oct 2023 to Jun 2024

$\frac{9}{12}\times8000=6000$

- Subtract the prepaid expense

$29600-6000=23600$

- Halve the amount

$\frac{1}{2}\times23600=11800$

Calculate the depreciation charge for factory machinery

- Calculate the net book value

$80000-35000=45000$

- Multiply by the percentage

$25 \% \times 45000 = 11250$

> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problem_md:
Sara has now been asked to supply a local drama school with theatrical costumes. The drama school would place an order with Sara each month and would require 60 days credit.

**REQUIRED**

Advise Sara whether she should start supplying the drama school with costumes. Justify your answer by providing advantages **and **disadvantages of supplying the costumes.
parts.solution_md:
If Sara agrees to this request, then there would be guaranteed work each month **[1]**. And if she gets a good reputation, she might be able to make similar arrangements with other schools **[1]**. However, Sara might not have the capacity to complete this order alongside the orders of her existing customers **[1]**. Also, allowing 60 days credit will have a negative impact on her liquidity **[1] **as she will be waiting nearly two months to receive payment.

Sara should decline this request **[1]** and try to negotiate better credit terms.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 5 marks in total:
> 
> - 1 mark for your **decision**.
> - Maximum 4 marks for **advantages **and **disadvantages **of supplying the costumes.
> 
>   - Up to 3 marks for **advantages**.
>   - Up to 3 marks for **disadvantages**.
> 
> **Advantages** may include:
> 
> - This is a guaranteed sale which will increase revenue
> - It might increase the profit
> - There is guaranteed monthly work
> - There is potential to replicate this deal with other schools
> - Other valid advantages are accepted
> 
> **Disadvantages** may include:
> 
> - Allowing 60 days credit will have a negative impact on liquidity
> - Sara might not have the capacity in the factory to store the costumes
> - Sara might not be able to supply the costumes to the school as well as uphold her other work with existing customers
> - This might increase the cost of production
> - Other valid disadvantages are accepted

2. Heat, light and power is to be apportioned 4/5 to the factory and 1/5 to the office.
3. Rates and insurance is to be apportioned 3/5 to the factory and 2/5 to the office. Insurance of \$4440 has been paid for the year to 31 December 2023.
4. At 31 July 2023, a factory repair, \$644, was unpaid and no adjustment had been made.
5. Factory equipment is depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method.

parts.problem_md:
Hilary is considering stopping buying any finished goods for resale and instead increasing the production at her factory.

**REQUIRED**

Advise Hilary whether she should sell only production from her own factory and increase the amount produced. Justify your answer by providing arguments for and against selling only production from her own factory and increasing the amount produced.
parts.solution_md:
If Hilary stopped buying finished goods from suppliers, then she will no longer have to rely on suppliers being able to provide the goods **[1]**. She might be able to produce the goods in her own factory for cheaper and make more profit **[1]**. Also, there is a significant amount of finished goods purchased from suppliers which are being returned **[1]**.

If Hilary did increase the amount that she produces, then she might not have the space in the factory to meet the demands **[1]**.

I'd advise Hilary that she should sell only production from her own factory **[1]**, as this has more benefits.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 5 marks in total:
> 
> - 1 mark for your **decision**.
> - Maximum 4 marks for **arguments for **and **arguments against **selling only production from Hilary's factory.
> 
>   - Up to 3 marks for **arguments for**.
>   - Up to 3 marks for **arguments against**.
> 
> **Arguments for **may include:
> 
> - Hilary will not have to rely on suppliers and has more control of her inventory levels
> - Hilary might be able to make better quality goods in her factory
> - It might be cheaper to produce her own goods
> - Hilary would have more control over the cost
> - There is a high number of purchased goods which are being returned
> - Other valid arguments for are accepted
> 
> **Arguments against **may include:
> 
> - The cost of production will increase
> - Hilary might need to purchase additional factory equipment
> - Hilary might not have the space in the factory to meet the demand
> - The quality of the goods currently purchased from the supplier might be higher than the quality of the goods produced in her factory
> - Other valid arguments against are accepted

parts.problem_md:
Salman is considering converting some of his office space into additional factory capacity.

Advise Salman whether he should convert some of his premises from office use to factory use. Justify your answer by providing arguments for and against this conversion of office space into additional factory capacity
parts.solution_md:
If Salman converts some of his office space to factory use then he might not need to purchase finished goods **[1]** and can manufacture all the goods. Salman has sufficient money in the bank to pay for the conversion **[1]**.

However, Salman might have to purchase additional factory equipment for the new space **[1]**. Salman might need all the office space for office purposes **[1]**.

Salman should convert some of his office space for factory use **[1]** because there is potential to increase profits.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 5 marks in total:
> 
> - 1 mark for your **decision**.
> - Maximum 4 marks for **advantages **and **disadvantages **of converting office space for factory use.
> 
>   - Up to 3 marks for **advantages **of converting office space for factory use.
>   - Up to 3 marks for **disadvantages **of converting office space for factory use.
> 
> **Advantages **may include:
> 
> - Salman might not need to purchase finished goods
> - Salman has the money in the bank for the conversion
> - The business might be more profitable with more space
> - The manufacturing part of the business appears to be profitable
> - Other valid advantages are accepted
> 
> **Disadvantages **may include:
> 
> - Salman might have to purchase additional factory equipment
> - The space might be needed for office purposes
> - The business might be unable to sell the extra manufactured goods
> - The conversion could be expensive
> - There might be more profitable uses of the money in the bank
> - Other valid disadvantages are accepted

parts.problem_md:
Yasmin opened a garment factory on 1 May 2016.

Yasmin is hoping to decrease her cost of production in the future. She thinks that if she spends a further \$25 000 on factory machinery she will be able to reduce the costs of direct labour by one third.

**REQUIRED **

Advise Yasmin whether or not she should buy the extra factory machinery. Justify your answer with **two** advantages and **two** disadvantages of your advice.
parts.solution_md:
If Yasmin buys the extra factory machinery then direct labour would reduce by \$10 767 each year **[1]**. This would increase the yearly profit **[1] **provided the selling price does not decrease.

However, the depreciation of the factory machinery would increase by \$5 000 per year **[1]**. There might also be costs incurred due to possible redundancies **[1]**.

Yasmin should purchase the extra factory machinery **[1]** to maximise her profit.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 5 marks in total:
> 
> - 1 mark for your **decision**.
> - Maximum 4 marks for **advantages **and **disadvantages **of buying the extra factory machinery.
> 
>   - Up to 2 marks for **advantages **of buying the extra factory machinery.
>   - Up to 3 marks for **disadvantages **of buying the extra factory machinery.
> 
> **Advantages **may include:
> 
> - Direct labour costs would reduce by \$10 767 a year
> - The cost of production would reduce by \$5 767 a pear
> - The profit for the year would increase provided the selling price does not decrease
> - Other valid advantages are accepted
> 
> **Disadvantages **may include:
> 
> - The depreciation of factory machinery would increase by \$5 000 a year
> - The costs for repairs and electricity would increase
> - If Yasmin pays \$25 000 from her bank then this will reduce her available cash
> - If Yasmin buys the machinery on credit then there will be finance costs
> - There might be redundancy costs
> - There might not be enough staff to deal with the demand and to cover absence
> - It might be difficult to hire more staff in the future
> - Other valid disadvantages are accepted

parts.problem_md:
Fozia opened a factory manufacturing wheelchairs on 1 May 2022. Fozia is considering reducing the number of wheelchairs she manufactures and instead buying in finished goods from a supplier.

**REQUIRED**

Advise Fozia whether she should start buying in finished goods from a supplier. Justify your answer by providing arguments for and against buying in finished goods and reducing the amount she manufactures.
parts.solution_md:
Fozia would save on storage costs **[1]** if she buys finished goods from a supplier. Fozia can save time **[1]** and buy in finished goods when she needs them.

Fozia would not have control over the quality **[1]** of the bought goods. Buying in goods might create job losses **[1] **which could damage the reputation of her business.

Fozia should continue manufacturing her own goods **[1]** as the advantages of buying in goods do not outweigh the disadvantages.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 5 marks in total:
> 
> - 1 mark for your **decision**.
> - Maximum 4 marks for **advantages **and **disadvantages **of buying in finished goods.
> 
>   - Up to 3 marks for **advantages **of buying in finished goods.
>   - Up to 3 marks for **disadvantages **of buying in finished goods.
> 
> **Advantages **may include:
> 
> - No need to maintain/manufacture inventory of raw materials
> - Saves storage and production costs
> - May be cheaper to buy in bulk from suppliers
> - Increasing profit margins
> - Saves time and resources
> - Can focus on sales and marketing
> - Any other valid advantage
> 
> **Disadvantages **may include:
> 
> - Loss of control over quality
> - Finished goods may not meet standards
> - Supplier may increase prices or fail to deliver
> - It might cause job losses
> - May lose unique selling point if goods are no longer self-manufactured
> - Any other valid disadvantage
